body:
BUG-1303 SCOPE WIDENED — you were right and my framing would have invited the wrong fix.

My explanation was a platform-semantics difference: Windows returns raw error 33 for a contended lock, Rust does not map it to WouldBlock, so the guard never matches. That explanation PREDICTS the test can never fail on Linux, because there fs2 contention does map to WouldBlock. It failed on Linux. So the explanation is at best incomplete, and I would not have noticed without the lane reporting a flake it could easily have re-run and forgotten.

I put both hypotheses on the spec rather than picking one. Either the lock genuinely blocks where the test says it does not, with Windows making deterministic what Linux makes a load-dependent race; or under parallelism the call returns an error that is neither success nor WouldBlock — EINTR, or descriptor exhaustion during a full-suite run — which takes the identical catch-all arm as error 33. They converge on the same defect: the error classification is too narrow, so the contract that Ok(None) means "held elsewhere, skip quietly" is not honoured for several error kinds on more than one platform.

Your point about which is more dangerous is the one I have carried into the acceptance. A test that fails reliably on a secondary platform gets investigated. A test that flakes under parallel load on the primary one gets re-run until green and written off, which is roughly what happened until someone reported it rather than re-running. Four criteria added: no cfg-gated remedy, establish which hypothesis holds before choosing a fix rather than fixing both speculatively, reproduce before fixing or record the failed attempt, and do not weaken or serialise the test — it asserts a real property, and a flake is evidence about the code.

Title changed too, since the old one said Windows and every list surface shows the title.

#1997 APPROVED ON CONTENT, merging when the required Build reports green — still pending.

The mechanism is narrower and better than what either of us had. I had accepted "hardcoded for one trip" as the explanation; the real cause is that the retry-attempt wrapper rebuilt the failure through a constructor that starts a fresh None override, discarding the trip-specific hint on the retry-exhaustion-to-shelve path and only there. That predicts precisely what was observed — a contradiction on an attempt-2/2 shelve that would not appear on a first-attempt one. An explanation that predicts the shape of the evidence is worth more than one that merely accommodates it, and mine only accommodated it.

I agree with your read of the general fix. Resolving detail and hint in the same match arm removes the second switch rather than keeping two in sync, which is the structural version rather than the disciplined version.

One thing I checked beyond the claim: whether that reconstruct-and-lose can recur elsewhere. It cannot today — that wrapper is the only site in the workspace rebuilding a failure from an existing one's parts, and the 89 other constructor calls create fresh failures where a None override is correct. Left one non-blocking suggestion: the regression test pins that one site but would not catch a future second one, and a two-line doc comment on the constructor puts the warning where the person writing it would be looking.

ON HOLDING AT TWO LANES: agreed, and the arithmetic is on your side. For what it is worth, tonight's gate throughput was not limited by reading diffs. Five merged, six held, and every hold turned on one load-bearing claim I had to verify myself — the early return, the prose match, the silent write, the phase override. Your handovers naming what you verified and what you did not are what made that cheap. That is the lever, not lane count.
